findings.problem: The live segment cannot hold the committed match. Live game > Match and report sets 'A match is 20 rounds (configurable)' and the Live success criterion requires 'a 20-round match completes', but the run sheet gives the live match 2:30 to 4:15, which is 105 s. That is about 5 s per round for a spoken countdown, a shoot-to-reveal round trip of up to 1.5 s and a spoken taunt, with nothing left for typing the name, handing the laptop to a classmate, or the 'planned moment' of switching to Personal mid-demo.
findings.remedy: Choose the demo match length and a per-round time budget that fit the live slot (for example 8-10 rounds, or a fixed split such as 5 rounds before and 5 after the Personal switch), make taunts and captions skippable in demo mode, and change the Live success criterion and the run sheet together. If 20 rounds stays as the default, label it practice or viva mode and give the run sheet its own shorter value.

findings.problem: The central live promise is unsupported and has no fallback. 'What Makes This Cool' says the bot's win rate 'climbs above the 33% luck line as it learns them', but the only evidence is human-versus-human play with random pairwise matching (Datasets item 2); nothing measures humans against a bot that counters their last move. Even if the 45% accuracy holds, a 20-round match has a standard deviation of about 11 points, so roughly 1 match in 8 ends at or below 33% (6 or fewer wins of 20) and about 1 in 4 at or below 35%, and the first rounds without history make it worse. The Success Criteria set no bot-performance expectation and the run sheet has no line for a match the bot loses.
findings.remedy: Restate the promise as an expectation with its variance (about 45% expected, +/-11 points over 20 rounds). Add a pre-demo pilot of several classmate matches against the bot to measure the real human-versus-bot win rate. Script what the presenter says and shows when the bot loses (for example the replay-through-every-brain table, or cumulative results over several matches, as the evidence instead of a single match).

findings.problem: The Personal brain is never defined, yet it carries measured claims and a planned demo moment. The Live game section calls it 'an online model that learns only from this player' and Part 2 reports 'Measured today: 46.1% over the first 50 rounds, 49.4% over rounds 50-150, 53.2% over rounds 150-300', but there is no algorithm, feature set, update rule or cold-start rule, so the figures cannot be reproduced. A model that starts empty reaching 46.1% in its first 50 rounds, roughly level with the 45.3% of models trained on 72 players, suggests a prior or a very small context set that is not stated. It maps to no lab algorithm (Premise 1) and cannot meet the 'explain every line' promise. All reported windows start at 50 rounds, while the live match is 20 rounds, so behaviour in the rounds the audience will see is unmeasured.
findings.remedy: Specify the Personal brain (features, model and update rule, cold-start or prior), commit the script that produced the three window figures, report its accuracy over the first 10 and first 20 rounds, and name the lab algorithm it corresponds to for the viva. If it is no better than the global brains within 20 rounds, change the planned switch moment or the match length accordingly.

findings.problem: Gesture capture is under-specified for real play. Round flow step 3 grabs 'one frame' at 'shoot' and only 'no hand found' triggers the 'Show me your hand' replay. A frame taken at the instant of the throw can catch a mid-motion hand; any detected hand is forced into rock, paper or scissors (a thumbs-up or half-formed shape still gets a label, with no confidence threshold); and nothing says which hand is used when two are in view. At the stated tolerance of 9 in 10 correct throws, about 2 rounds of a 20-round match can be misread, and each misread is scored, appended to the history, and fed to the Personal brain and the habits report.
findings.remedy: Define the capture rule (for example read a short burst after 'shoot' and take the majority or most confident prediction, single hand only), add a confidence threshold that reuses the existing 'Show me your hand' replay, and add a quick 'that was misread' correction that fixes score and history. State these in Round flow and add a matching success criterion (misread rate measured across several people).

findings.problem: The round-history lifecycle is missing. Part 2 features need 'the player's last two moves, the opponent's last move and the last two results' and the data notes say 'the first round has no previous move', but Round flow step 1 only says 'using this player's history so far'. Undefined: what the bot plays in rounds 1 and 2 when history is shorter than the feature set; whether history resets per match, persists when the same name is typed again, or is polluted when another classmate takes over without a new name; how a stay/up/down ('relative') prediction is converted to an absolute counter-move; and whether no-hand replays or corrected misreads write to the history.
findings.remedy: Add a short rule list to the Live game section: the cold-start move and fallback brain for rounds 1-2, the history scope (per match, per typed name, reset on name change), the relative-to-absolute conversion with one worked example, and that replays and rejected throws never enter the history.

findings.problem: The Eyes model is trained on CGI renders but judged on one real hand, with no stated feature invariances and a fallback triggered by the wrong signal. Datasets item 1 uses 2,520 + 372 square 300x300 CGI images and the features are only 'relative to the wrist and normalised for hand size'. Nothing handles rotation or tilt, left versus right hand, a mirrored webcam preview, or the aspect-ratio difference of a 4:3 or 16:9 frame when landmarks are normalised separately by width and height, and the CSV stores no handedness. The only live guard is 'Krish's hand ... at least 9 of 10 throws' (one person, 10 throws), and the own-recordings fallback in Open Questions is triggered only by a CGI detection rate under about 90%, not by poor accuracy on real hands. If own recordings replace the CGI data, the '95% on the public data' criterion no longer applies and nothing says how Part 1 changes.
findings.remedy: State the invariances to build into the features (rotate to a wrist-to-knuckle axis, mirror to one handedness, use pixel or world coordinates so distances are not skewed). Widen the live criterion (at least 3 people including a left-handed one, both hands, 2 lighting conditions, 10 throws per gesture). Add a live-accuracy trigger for the own-recordings fallback, and say how recorded data would enter Part 1 and which success criterion then applies.

findings.problem: Part 1 and Part 2 apply opposite leakage standards, which leaves the Eyes criterion ambiguous. Part 2 insists on a player-level split because 'a random split would leak information', but Part 1 defaults to 'An 80/20 stratified split' of CGI renders (a random split can put near-duplicate renders on both sides, to be checked) and leaves the official TensorFlow split as 'the builder's call', even though the CSV stores 'the original split'. The success criterion 'at least 95% test accuracy on the public data' does not say which test set it means, so a leaked 80/20 score could satisfy it without showing generalisation.
findings.remedy: Decide now: make the official TensorFlow train/test split the headline result (or group by source if known), keep 80/20 only as a clearly labelled lab-style demo, state which one the 95% criterion uses, and have Part 1 explain the leakage point as Part 2 does.

findings.problem: Find-S is committed to a setting where it is likely to degenerate. Part 1 runs Find-S on 'the finger booleans' derived from landmark geometry, with 'scissors' as the target, and 'prints the hypothesis after each example'. Find-S assumes noise-free data and a conjunctive concept: one misjudged boolean among hundreds of scissors examples turns that attribute to '?' permanently, so the result can collapse to an all-'?' hypothesis. The up/down rule ('tip farther from the wrist than its middle joint') is not defined for the thumb, which has a different joint chain, and printing after every one of hundreds of examples is unreadable. The run sheet features Find-S at 0:30 with no plan for failure.
findings.remedy: Decide the Find-S input (for example the four non-thumb fingers, a verified clean subset, or a threshold that keeps the booleans stable), define the thumb rule, print only the examples that change the hypothesis, and decide in advance whether a degenerate result is shown deliberately as the story (Find-S fails on noisy data). Test it in the spike so the run sheet can rely on the outcome.

findings.problem: Approach B has two inconsistent triggers. Approaches Considered says B 'gets built only if the Colab camera test in Next Steps step 1 fails, or is too slow to feel live', but Open Questions says that if venue internet 'isn't reliable, Approach B becomes necessary'. The second condition can arise after step 1 passes, has no decision point or deadline, and falls outside the first rule; listing it as an open question does not reconcile the two.
findings.remedy: Replace both statements with one trigger list (spike failure, latency over budget, venue connectivity unconfirmed by a stated date) and give the venue question an owner and a date, so the B decision is not left until late in the build.

findings.problem: The Assignment cannot produce the evidence its interpretation relies on. Thirty rounds against a friend gives about 10 post-loss throws (roughly one round in three), so each friend's 'repeat after losing' rate rests on about 10 events and a 95% interval of roughly +/-30 points. 53% and 33% cannot be told apart, yet either outcome is read as good news ('I tested it on my friends too', or 'an even better viva answer: one study's average doesn't fit every person'). Both conclusions would be unsupported if said aloud.
findings.remedy: Raise the sample (about 100 rounds per friend, roughly 33 post-loss events, or pool several friends), record throws in the same columns as the study data so the logs can be replayed through the live engine, report 'k of n' counts rather than percentages, and fix beforehand what result changes what Krish says. Drop the 'better viva answer' claim unless the sample can support it.

findings.problem: Nothing guards against train/serve mismatch, the most likely silent failure of the live game. Offline, features come from the CSVs (Part 2) and from cv2.imread plus a BGR to RGB step (Datasets item 1); live, they are rebuilt separately from 'this player's history so far' and from a browser frame decoded by OpenCV. A different move encoding, result perspective, relative-to-absolute rotation, colour order or mirroring raises no error: the bot would just play near 33% or mislabel hands. The Success Criteria check only a 9-of-10 hand test and that 'a 20-round match completes'.
findings.remedy: Require one shared feature-building function used by both the notebook and the live engine, and add parity checks to the Success Criteria: replay a held-out player's 300 rounds through the live engine and match the offline accuracy within noise, and push saved test images through the live decode path to get the same landmarks and labels as the CSV.

findings.problem: Two figures for the same fact differ. Datasets item 2 says 'rock is chosen 35.7% of the time' while Premise 3 and the baseline table give 'always rock' as 35.6%. The gap probably comes from excluding first-round rows, but the document never says so, in a project whose pitch is honest baselines.
findings.remedy: State the row set behind each number (all 21,600 rows versus only rows with enough history) or use a single figure.

findings.problem: The Datasets column list includes an 'input' column that is never defined or given a role. If it encodes the current opponent move or round outcome, using it as a feature would leak the label.
findings.remedy: Define the `input` column in the data notes and state whether it is excluded from the features.

findings.problem: Next Steps step 1 tests 'the MediaPipe 1.1.1 HandLandmarker API', but the install cell in Notebook structure 0 is an unpinned 'pip install mediapipe', and the version number is not sourced anywhere in the document. A fresh Colab runtime can resolve a different version than the one the spike validated, and an install that upgrades preinstalled packages can force a runtime restart that would interrupt 'Run all'.
findings.remedy: Pin the exact version the spike validates (and the hand_landmarker.task URL or checksum) in the install cell, cite where 1.1.1 comes from, and record in the spike whether a restart is needed after the install.

findings.problem: The notebook never says how the CSVs reach a fresh Colab runtime. Parts 1 and 2 'load the CSV by default' and the Success Criteria require 'Run all' to work on a fresh runtime, but 'Open in Colab' opens only the notebook, and whether the repo is public is still an Open Question.
findings.remedy: Add a first-cell data fetch (clone the public repo or download the two CSVs from raw URLs) with a clear error message if it fails, and settle the public-repo question before the notebook is built.

findings.problem: Viva prep says VIVA_GUIDE.md is 'also published as a readable web page', but the Distribution Plan lists only the repo contents with 'No CI' and describes no hosting or build step.
findings.remedy: Either add the hosting step (for example GitHub Pages, which needs the public repo) to the Distribution Plan or drop the web page.

findings.problem: The live screen is specified by reference to material that is not in the document: 'mockup B, Face-off, from the brainstorm' and 'mockup C's table'. A reader or the next engineering review cannot see them, and the bot's name CHANAKYA appears without introduction.
findings.remedy: Save the mockups into the repo (for example docs/mockups) and link them, or replace them with a short text wireframe, and introduce the bot persona once.

findings.problem: The match rules behind the screen are undefined. The Face-off screen shows 'Health bars', but nothing says what drains them, how ties and a tied match are scored, who wins the match, or whether reaching zero ends the match early, which would conflict with a fixed 20-round match.
findings.remedy: Define the rules (damage per round, tie handling, match winner, early finish) in one short paragraph.

findings.problem: Small-sample statistics are presented as findings. The match report shows 'repeat rate after a loss, tie and win', 'which way they cycle', a replay 'through every brain to show which one read the player best', and a 'most unpredictable human today' leaderboard, all from a 20-round match with about 6-7 transitions per result type. Gaps of 1-2 points between brains are far below the roughly 11-point match noise, the leaderboard metric is not defined, and this sits against Premise 3, 'Honest baselines everywhere'.
findings.remedy: Define the leaderboard metric, show counts as k of n with a 'small sample' note, present the brain replay as illustrative rather than a ranking, or cut the leaderboard.

findings.problem: Several Success Criteria cannot be checked as written. The Brain bar 'at least 44% on unseen players (45.3% measured)' names no protocol (mean of 5-fold GroupKFold or a single GroupShuffleSplit) and leaves a 1.3-point margin; the Eyes live test is one person and 10 throws; 'under about 1.5 s' and 'under about 5 minutes' are hedged; 'the bot's move is locked before the frame is captured' has no test; and 'answer a 10-question mock viva' has no pass mark.
findings.remedy: Give each criterion its protocol, exact threshold and pass mark. Make the lock testable (the engine stores the locked move in Python and the throw handler receives only a round id) and add it as an automated check.

findings.problem: The 5-minute 'Run all' budget is unproven. Part 2 quotes 'about 30-40 s' per RBF fit on 21K rows, so one 5-fold pass is already about 2-3 minutes, and a grid search or learning curve on the full data is far beyond the budget. The stated mitigation ('a subsample or a small grid') is not specified, and the 45.3% measured for SVM (RBF) used full data, so the reported figure will change.
findings.remedy: Fix the subsample size and grids, give each section a time budget, time a full run on a fresh Colab runtime in the spike, and report the subsampled SVM figure instead of 45.3%.

findings.problem: The Colab-specific risks are tested too narrowly and too late. The spike covers MediaPipe detection on 50 CGI images (not stratified by class) and one invokeFunction round trip. It omits detection on real webcam frames, getUserMedia permission inside the Colab output iframe on the demo laptop's browser, speechSynthesis voices and audio over HDMI or Wondercast, and who runs it (it needs Krish's Colab and camera). The next Colab test is Next Steps step 9, after the JS widget, speech and report are built blind.
findings.remedy: Expand the spike to those items and name who runs it on which laptop and browser. Add Colab checkpoints with Krish after steps 5 and 6, plus a stubbed invokeFunction harness so the widget can be exercised outside Colab.

findings.problem: The live label shares one channel with the throw. 'Between rounds, a live label refreshes a few times a second; the builder sets the rate' sends frames through the same invokeFunction path and kernel that must answer the 'shoot' call within the stated 1.5 s. With no back-pressure rule, queued preview calls can delay the shoot call.
findings.remedy: Specify single-flight previews (skip a frame while one is in flight), a hard maximum rate, and previews paused during the countdown and throw. Test shoot latency with the preview running in the spike.

findings.problem: The reveal shows a percentage for every brain ('I predicted ROCK (62%)'), but the dropdown includes models with no or poor probability output: the Perceptron has no predict_proba, a Decision Tree gives coarse leaf frequencies, and an SVM needs probability=True, which adds an internal cross-validation to fitting 21K rows and strains the run-time budget. Part 1's 'predict one new sample with predict_proba' has the same gap for the Perceptron.
findings.remedy: State what the reveal shows per brain (omit the percentage for Perceptron and Random, or use a calibrated alternative) and budget the cost of SVM probabilities.

findings.problem: Part 2 feature encoding and target coding are unspecified. Part 1 uses 'a Pipeline with StandardScaler' and the lab-structure list names ColumnTransformer, but Part 2 lists Categorical NB, Decision Tree, Perceptron, Logistic Regression and SVM with no encoding, although Categorical NB needs non-negative integer codes and the linear models and SVM need one-hot features. The accuracy table does not say whether it was measured on absolute moves or on the stay/up/down target, and neither Part places ColumnTransformer.
findings.remedy: Specify the encoding per model (placing ColumnTransformer in Part 2) and state which target, absolute or relative, the table and the live brains use.

findings.problem: The Perceptron story is promised but never given. 'What Makes This Cool' says the Perceptron 'fails at the brain task for a reason worth explaining' (36.7%, close to always-rock at 35.6%), but no reason is stated. 'Not linearly separable' would not explain it, because Logistic Regression is also a linear model and scores 43.9%.
findings.remedy: State the explanation Krish will give (for example non-converging updates on noisy, non-separable labels, or no probabilistic output) and show the supporting evidence in the notebook, or drop the claim.

findings.problem: The headline statistic is attributed to the study but is the project's own calculation. The Problem Statement says 'in a 2014 study ... players repeated their previous move 52.7% of the time right after losing', while Datasets says 'Checked today' on a CSV produced by a custom R-file reader, and the opening line generalises it to 'people'. The pattern (52.7% repeats after a loss versus 36.0% after a win) is the reverse of the familiar win-stay, lose-shift heuristic, so examiners are likely to probe it, and no reproducible check is included.
findings.remedy: Say 'computed from the study's public data' (and cite where the paper reports it, if it does), add the check as a notebook cell or tools/ assert so the figure is reproducible, and add a viva note on the sample (72 players, one lab design).

findings.problem: The privacy statement is narrower than the behaviour. 'Frames are processed in memory and never saved' describes the notebook's code, but every frame of a classmate's face leaves the laptop for a Google-hosted VM (Constraints: Colab runs on Google's servers), nothing tells the player so, and the notebook is committed 'saved with outputs' to a repo that may be public, so a debug cell showing a frame or a typed name would be published.
findings.remedy: Add a one-line disclosure and consent prompt before the camera starts, reword the statement to what is true, and add a pre-commit step that clears live-game outputs and checks the .ipynb contains no frames or names.

findings.problem: The browser-to-Python boundary has no validation. Python callbacks receive a frame, a brain choice, a round id and a typed name through invokeFunction, but the document sets no frame size or format limit, no allow-list for the brain choice, and does not say names are rendered as text, so a malformed frame or a name containing HTML can break the callback or the page.
findings.remedy: Specify that Python validates inputs (maximum frame size, reject undecodable images, brain id from an allow-list, name length) and that the widget renders names with textContent, not as HTML.

findings.problem: Widget failure states are not specified: camera permission denied or no camera, getUserMedia blocked, kernel disconnected or busy, speech unavailable. The only error path is 'no hand found'. A denied permission blocks the whole live segment with no on-screen explanation and no non-camera way to continue.
findings.remedy: List the failure states with the on-screen message for each, and add a keyboard or click throw mode so a match, the report and the viva demo still run without the camera.

findings.problem: There is no priority order or cut line while the deadline is an open question ('When is the presentation? That decides how much polish fits'). Next Steps commit to everything: leaderboard, spoken taunts, habit and cycle analysis, replay through every brain, a seven-plus-brain dropdown, accessibility, a web page, and a line-by-line guide for every cell with 50+ Q&A. Several cannot surface in the run sheet (the match report gets 30 s).
findings.remedy: Add a must/should/could ordering with a minimum viable demo (Parts 1-2, a simple live match and the guide) and name the first items to cut if the date is short.

findings.problem: Fallback artifacts are missing from the Distribution Plan. Approach B 'reuses the trained models' in a local OpenCV window, but the repo lists only the notebook, data/, tools/, the guide and a README: no saved models, local runner or local copy of hand_landmarker.task. B also runs against Krish's stated rule 'i have to directly present my project on google colab' without saying whether the professor accepts it. Premise 4 ('saved with outputs') covers a misbehaving cell, not lost internet or a recycled Colab runtime, where trained models live only in kernel memory and Part 3 needs a full re-run of up to the whole 5-minute slot.
findings.remedy: State in the Distribution Plan what each fallback needs: persisted models, a local runner and model file if B is kept, an offline HTML or PDF export of the executed notebook, and a fast-restart cell that loads saved models. Add one line on whether presenting B satisfies the professor's Colab rule.
